Egypt.0: Farming villages spread along the Nile from c. 5000 BC as the Sahara dried and people crowded toward the river. Predynastic cultures such as the Badarian and Naqada built chiefdoms, traded widely, and buried elites with rich goods. Around 3100 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under one king, and hieroglyphic writing appeared.
Egypt.1: Kings of the Early Dynastic period and the Old Kingdom (c. 2686 to 2181 BC) ruled a centralized state from Memphis, treating the pharaoh as a god-king. They built the Step Pyramid of Djoser and the Giza pyramids. Royal power then fragmented in the First Intermediate Period until Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt c. 2055 BC, founding the Middle Kingdom.
Egypt.2: The Middle Kingdom produced classic literature and built forts in Nubia, but foreign Hyksos rulers later seized the Nile Delta. Theban kings expelled them c. 1550 BC and founded the New Kingdom, an empire reaching into the Levant and Nubia. Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II reigned before power faded after c. 1070 BC.
Egypt.3: In the Third Intermediate Period Egypt was divided among Libyan-descended dynasties and powerful priests of Amun at Thebes. Kushite kings from Nubia ruled as pharaohs from c. 744 BC until Assyria invaded in 671 BC and drove them out. Psamtik I then reunited the country in 664 BC, founding the Saite dynasty with Greek mercenary help.
Egypt.4: The Saite pharaohs, especially Amasis, presided over a prosperous Egypt that welcomed Greek merchants at the trading town of Naukratis. In 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses defeated the last Saite ruler at Pelusium and made Egypt a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Darius I later completed a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea.
Egypt.5: Egypt was a Persian satrapy, paying tribute to distant Achaemenid kings while temples and local life continued much as before. Egyptians revolted repeatedly, notably under Inaros c. 460 BC with Athenian help. The Greek historian Herodotus toured the country around this time, and in 404 BC Amyrtaeus won independence for native rule again.
Egypt.6: Native pharaohs of the 30th dynasty, such as Nectanebo II, built temples until Persia reconquered Egypt in 343 BC. Alexander the Great took the country without a fight in 332 BC and founded Alexandria on the coast. After his death his general Ptolemy took control and declared himself king in 305 BC, founding the Ptolemaic dynasty.
Egypt.7: The Greek-speaking Ptolemies ruled Egypt as pharaohs while running it as a royal estate taxed for grain. Alexandria, with its Great Library, Museum and Lighthouse, became the intellectual capital of the Hellenistic world, home to scholars like Eratosthenes. Wars with the Seleucids over Syria and a long revolt in Upper Egypt strained the kingdom.
Egypt.8: Ptolemaic power weakened through dynastic feuds, rebellions and costly wars, and Rome increasingly arbitrated Egyptian affairs. The Rosetta Stone (196 BC) recorded a royal decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, reflecting a mixed society. Alexandria remained a rich trading city, but the dynasty survived more by Roman favor than by its own strength.
Egypt.9: Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler, allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony to keep Egypt independent. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BC, and after Cleopatra's death in 30 BC Rome annexed Egypt. It became a special province under the emperor's personal control, shipping huge quantities of grain to Rome.
Egypt.10: As a Roman province governed by a prefect, Egypt was the empire's breadbasket, and Alexandria was its second city. Greek-speaking elites, Egyptian farmers and a large Jewish community lived side by side, sometimes violently, as in the Alexandrian riots of AD 38. According to tradition, Christianity was brought to Alexandria by Saint Mark.
Egypt.11: Roman Egypt prospered from grain, papyrus and Red Sea trade with India. A Jewish revolt in 115 to 117 destroyed much of Alexandria's Jewish community. The scholar Claudius Ptolemy wrote his astronomy and geography in Alexandria, Emperor Hadrian toured the Nile, and a Christian school of learning grew in the city.
Egypt.12: Under Rome, Egyptians became Roman citizens in 212, but heavy taxes and the empire's third-century crisis brought hardship. Christians faced persecutions while thinkers such as Origen shaped theology in Alexandria. Zenobia of Palmyra briefly seized Egypt c. 270, and around this time Saint Anthony retreated into the desert, launching Christian monasticism.
Egypt.13: Diocletian reorganized Roman Egypt and fiercely persecuted Christians in 303, but Christianity soon became the favored, then official, faith. Alexandria's bishops Athanasius and Arius fought over doctrine, and Pachomius founded communal monasteries in Upper Egypt. In 391 Christians destroyed the Serapeum, and after 395 Egypt belonged to the Eastern Roman Empire.
Egypt.14: Egypt was a wealthy province of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, ruled from Constantinople. Religious conflict was intense: a Christian mob killed the philosopher Hypatia in 415, and after the Council of Chalcedon in 451 most Egyptian Christians rejected imperial doctrine, forming the Coptic Church and loosening loyalty to the emperors.
Egypt.15: Byzantine emperors, especially Justinian, relied on Egyptian grain while trying to impose their version of Christianity on the Copts. The last temple of Isis at Philae was closed c. 537. The devastating Plague of Justinian reached the empire through Egypt's port of Pelusium in 541, killing large numbers across the Mediterranean.
Egypt.16: Sasanian Persia occupied Egypt from 619 to 628 before the Byzantine emperor Heraclius won it back. Weakened and divided by religious quarrels, Egypt fell to Arab Muslim armies under Amr ibn al-As around 641. The conquerors founded a garrison city, Fustat, near the future Cairo, and Egypt became a province of the caliphate.
Egypt.17: Egypt was governed by Umayyad and, after 750, Abbasid caliphs through appointed governors. Arabic replaced Greek in government records from 706, and heavy taxes on non-Muslims provoked several Coptic revolts. Most Egyptians were still Christians, but Arabic language and Islam were slowly spreading through cities and countryside.
Egypt.18: Abbasid rule continued, but local tensions ran high; the Bashmurian revolt of Copts in the Delta was crushed in 831. In 868 the Turkish governor Ahmad ibn Tulun made Egypt effectively independent, building an army and the great Mosque of Ibn Tulun. The Tulunids extended their rule into Syria before the Abbasids reclaimed control in 905.
Egypt.19: After a period of Abbasid and Ikhshidid governors, the Shia Fatimid Caliphate from North Africa conquered Egypt in 969. The Fatimids founded Cairo as their new capital and the al-Azhar mosque as a center of learning. Egypt became the seat of a rival caliphate challenging Baghdad, wealthy from Mediterranean and Red Sea trade.
Egypt.20: The Fatimid caliphs ruled from Cairo over Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz. The erratic caliph al-Hakim destroyed Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009. A severe famine and civil strife in the 1060s nearly toppled the state, until the general Badr al-Jamali restored order and rebuilt Cairo's walls and gates.
Egypt.21: Weakened Fatimid caliphs faced Crusader states on their borders. A Kurdish commander, Saladin, became vizier and in 1171 ended the Fatimid line, restoring Sunni Islam and founding the Ayyubid dynasty. From Egypt he united Muslim Syria, built Cairo's Citadel, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
Egypt.22: Ayyubid sultans repelled Crusades aimed at Egypt, including Louis IX's invasion in 1249 to 1250. Their slave-soldier regiments, the Mamluks, then seized power in 1250 and defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260. Sultans such as Baybars hosted a figurehead Abbasid caliph in Cairo and expelled the last Crusaders from the Levant by 1291.
Egypt.23: The Mamluk Sultanate reached its peak under al-Nasir Muhammad, ruling Egypt and Syria from Cairo, the largest city of the Islamic world. Mosques, madrasas and markets flourished on the profits of the spice trade. The Black Death struck in 1347 to 1349, killing a large share of the population, and Circassian Mamluks took power in 1382.
Egypt.24: Mamluk Egypt struggled with recurring plague, falling farm output and costly factional fighting, while sultans taxed the lucrative spice trade between India and Europe. Timur sacked Mamluk Damascus in 1400. Sultan Qaitbay built fine monuments, but Portugal's sea route around Africa, opened in 1498, threatened Egypt's trade income.
Egypt.25: In 1517 the Ottoman sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluks and conquered Egypt, ending Cairo's role as an imperial capital. Egypt became a wealthy Ottoman province ruled by a pasha sent from Istanbul. Mamluk households survived as local landholding elites, and Cairo grew rich on the new coffee trade from Yemen.
Egypt.26: Egypt remained an Ottoman province, but real power shifted toward the Mamluk beys and rival military factions in Cairo. Governors from Istanbul came and went quickly while local grandees controlled tax farms and land. The coffee trade through Red Sea ports kept Cairo's merchants prosperous despite frequent political infighting.
Egypt.27: Ottoman authority over Egypt was largely nominal as Mamluk beys and Janissary factions competed for control of revenue. The Qazdughli household gradually rose to dominate Cairo's politics. Egypt's farmers still produced grain for the empire, and coffee and textile trade connected Cairo to markets across the Ottoman world.
Egypt.28: The Mamluk bey Ali Bey al-Kabir briefly broke from the Ottomans and invaded Syria c. 1770, before rivals Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey took over. In 1798 Napoleon invaded, won the Battle of the Pyramids, and brought scholars who studied the country. The British destroyed his fleet at the Nile, and French troops found the Rosetta Stone in 1799.
Egypt.29: After the French left in 1801, the Albanian officer Muhammad Ali took power in 1805 as Ottoman governor and ruled autonomously. He massacred the Mamluk leaders in 1811, built a modern army, monopolized trade and promoted cotton. He fought for the sultan in Arabia, conquered Sudan from 1820, and Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs in 1822.
Egypt.30: Muhammad Ali's armies fought in the Greek War of Independence and, under his son Ibrahim, seized Syria in 1831. European powers forced Egypt to withdraw in 1840, but the Ottomans granted his family hereditary rule. His factories, schools and conscription remade Egyptian society, though at heavy cost to peasants. He died in 1849.
Egypt.31: Muhammad Ali's successors Said and Ismail pursued grand modernization, aided by a cotton boom during the American Civil War. The Suez Canal, built with forced Egyptian labor, opened in 1869 and transformed world shipping. Ismail took the title Khedive in 1867 and rebuilt Cairo in European style, but borrowed heavily from European banks.
Egypt.32: Facing bankruptcy, Ismail sold Egypt's Suez Canal shares to Britain in 1875 and accepted European financial control. Colonel Urabi's nationalist revolt led Britain to invade and occupy Egypt in 1882, ruling behind the khedive. Egypt lost Sudan to the Mahdist uprising, then shared it with Britain after the reconquest of 1898.
Egypt.33: Britain's consul-general Lord Cromer effectively ran Egypt, balancing budgets and expanding irrigation, including the first Aswan Dam in 1902. Egyptians resented foreign control, especially after the Denshawai incident of 1906, when villagers were hanged after a clash with British officers. Nationalists like Mustafa Kamil built a growing independence movement.
Egypt.34: When the Ottomans joined the Central Powers in 1914, Britain declared Egypt a protectorate and turned it into a major base for the war in the Middle East. Wartime requisitions and forced labor caused deep anger. In 1919, after Britain exiled the nationalist Saad Zaghlul, a nationwide revolution erupted across classes and religions.
Egypt.35: Britain declared Egypt nominally independent in 1922 under King Fuad, while keeping control of defense, the Suez Canal and Sudan. A 1923 constitution created a parliament dominated by Zaghlul's Wafd party. Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, and in 1928 Hassan al-Banna founded the Muslim Brotherhood.
Egypt.36: Egypt's constitutional monarchy struggled with royal interference, the Great Depression and falling cotton prices. Young King Farouk took the throne in 1936, the same year an Anglo-Egyptian treaty reduced but did not end the British military presence. Mass movements like the Muslim Brotherhood and nationalist youth groups grew rapidly.
Egypt.37: Egypt was a key Allied base in the Second World War; British forces stopped the German advance at El Alamein in 1942 and forced a government on King Farouk. The Arab League was founded in Cairo in 1945. Defeat in the 1948 war against the new state of Israel discredited the monarchy and fueled unrest.
Egypt.38: Gamal Abdel Nasser and the Free Officers overthrew King Farouk in 1952 and created a republic. Nasser became a hero of Arab nationalism by nationalizing the Suez Canal, surviving the 1956 British, French and Israeli invasion, and briefly uniting with Syria in 1958. Land reform and Soviet aid for the Aswan High Dam followed.
Egypt.39: Nasser's Arab socialist state nationalized industry and expanded schools, while Egyptian troops fought a long war in Yemen. Israel's crushing victory in the 1967 Six-Day War cost Egypt the Sinai and shattered Nasser's prestige. The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970, ending the Nile flood, and Nasser died that year.
Egypt.40: Anwar Sadat succeeded Nasser, expelled Soviet advisers, and launched the 1973 October War, crossing the Suez Canal. He opened the economy to foreign investment and turned toward the United States. His Camp David accords led to a 1979 peace treaty with Israel, regaining Sinai but isolating Egypt in the Arab world.
Egypt.41: Islamist officers assassinated Sadat in 1981, and Hosni Mubarak became president, ruling under emergency law. Israel completed its withdrawal from Sinai in 1982, and Egypt gradually returned to the Arab League. Large American aid supported the army, while rapid population growth strained Cairo, jobs and housing.
Egypt.42: Mubarak joined the US-led coalition in the 1991 Gulf War, earning debt relief, and began market reforms. An Islamist insurgency targeted officials, Copts and tourists, culminating in the 1997 Luxor massacre before militants were crushed. The ruling party monopolized politics as Cairo's population swelled past ten million.
Egypt.43: Mubarak's long rule continued amid economic growth that benefited a narrow elite, and speculation that his son Gamal would succeed him. The 2005 elections allowed limited competition, and the Kefaya movement and labor strikes, including in Mahalla in 2008, showed rising discontent over prices, corruption and police abuse.
Egypt.44: Mass protests in Tahrir Square toppled Mubarak in 2011 during the Arab Spring. The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the 2012 election, but in 2013 the army under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi removed him and crushed his supporters. Sisi became president in 2014, expanded the Suez Canal, and ruled with tight control.
Egypt.45: President Sisi's government pressed on with megaprojects such as a New Administrative Capital and the Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza. Debt, inflation and sharp currency devaluations brought repeated IMF loans and hardship. Wars in Gaza and Sudan and Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping, which cut Suez Canal income, affected Egypt deeply.

North Africa.0: During the humid 'Green Sahara' period, hunters, fishers and later cattle herders lived across what is now desert, leaving rock art at sites like Tassili n'Ajjer. Along the Maghreb, the Iberomaurusian and Capsian cultures hunted and gathered snails and plants. Between c. 9000 and 4000 BC the Sahara dried, pushing people toward the coasts and oases.
North Africa.1: With the Sahara now largely desert, people of the Maghreb lived as herders of sheep, goats and cattle, with some farming near the coast. These were ancestors of the Berbers (Amazigh). Egyptian records describe western neighbors called Tehenu and Tjemehu, and Neolithic communities in Morocco had contacts across the Strait of Gibraltar.
North Africa.2: Libyan peoples such as the Libu and Meshwesh pressed on Egypt's western frontier, joining the Sea Peoples in an invasion repelled c. 1208 BC. Horses and chariots spread into the Sahara, appearing in rock art. Late in this era, Phoenician sailors from the Levant began setting up trading stops along the North African coast.
North Africa.3: Phoenicians from Tyre founded Carthage, traditionally in 814 BC, in what is now Tunisia, along with posts such as Utica and Lixus. Greek colonists from Thera founded Cyrene in Libya c. 631 BC. Inland, Berber peoples herded and farmed, while the Garamantes of the Fezzan began building an oasis society in the Sahara.
North Africa.4: Carthage became the leading Phoenician city of the west, building a trading empire across Sardinia, western Sicily, Spain and the African coast. It allied with the Etruscans against Greek rivals c. 540 BC and signed a treaty with Rome in 509 BC. Greek Cyrene grew rich exporting the medicinal plant silphium.
North Africa.5: Carthage suffered defeat by the Greeks of Syracuse at Himera in 480 BC, then turned inland to farm the fertile Tunisian countryside. Carthaginian navigators such as Hanno reportedly sailed down Africa's Atlantic coast. Herodotus described Libyan tribes and the Garamantes, who traded across the Sahara using horses and chariots.
North Africa.6: Carthage fought repeated wars with Syracuse for Sicily; the tyrant Agathocles even invaded Africa in 310 BC. The Punic city was a wealthy republic ruled by merchant aristocrats, with grand harbors. In the east, Cyrene fell under Ptolemaic Egypt c. 322 BC, while Numidian and Mauri Berber kingdoms took shape inland.
North Africa.7: Carthage clashed with Rome in the First and Second Punic Wars between 264 and 201 BC. Hannibal crossed the Alps and ravaged Italy, but Rome invaded Africa and defeated him at Zama in 202 BC. The Numidian king Masinissa, Rome's ally, emerged as a powerful Berber ruler at Carthage's expense.
North Africa.8: Masinissa's Numidia pressed Carthage until Rome destroyed the city in 146 BC and created the Province of Africa. Numidia's king Jugurtha fought Rome from 112 to 105 BC before being captured. Rome gained Cyrenaica by bequest in 96 BC, while Berber kingdoms ruled most of the interior.
North Africa.9: Julius Caesar defeated Pompey's allies and King Juba I of Numidia at Thapsus in 46 BC, expanding Roman Africa. Augustus refounded Carthage as a Roman colony, and North African grain began feeding Rome. In Mauretania (Morocco and western Algeria), the learned client king Juba II ruled with his wife Cleopatra Selene.
North Africa.10: Rome tightened its hold, crushing the long revolt of the Berber leader Tacfarinas in AD 17 to 24. Caligula executed King Ptolemy of Mauretania in 40, and his kingdom was annexed as two Roman provinces. Olive oil and grain estates expanded, and cities like Leptis Magna were adorned with Roman monuments.
North Africa.11: Roman North Africa enjoyed peace and prosperity, exporting grain, olive oil and pottery across the empire. Trajan founded the planned city of Timgad c. 100, and a legion guarded the frontier from Lambaesis. Latin culture flourished, producing writers like Apuleius, while Christianity began spreading in Carthage and other cities.
North Africa.12: Septimius Severus, born at Leptis Magna, became Roman emperor in 193 and lavished his hometown with buildings. African Christians such as Tertullian and Bishop Cyprian of Carthage, martyred in 258, shaped Latin theology. The great amphitheater at El Djem was built, but the empire's third-century crises brought revolts and strain.
North Africa.13: Under Diocletian's reforms North Africa remained a rich Roman region, now largely Christian. The Donatist schism split African churches bitterly for generations. Augustine, born in 354, became bishop of Hippo in 395 and one of Christianity's most influential thinkers, while Berber chiefs such as Firmus and Gildo revolted against imperial authority.
North Africa.14: The Germanic Vandals under Gaiseric crossed from Spain in 429 and took Carthage in 439, creating a kingdom that dominated the western Mediterranean. Augustine died in 430 as they besieged Hippo. The Arian Christian Vandals persecuted Catholics and sacked Rome in 455, while Berber kingdoms grew in the mountains and desert edges.
North Africa.15: Byzantine general Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533 to 534, restoring imperial rule over the coastlands. The Byzantines built fortresses but faced constant warfare with independent Berber (Moorish) kingdoms. Roman culture and Christianity persisted in cities, though much of the interior was now ruled by Berber chiefs.
North Africa.16: Arab Muslim armies invaded from Egypt from 647, defeating the Byzantines at Sufetula. Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan in 670 as a base, but Berber leaders, including Kusaila and the warrior queen Dihya (al-Kahina), fought back hard. Carthage fell in 698, and by c. 709 Arab rule reached the Atlantic.
North Africa.17: North Africa was a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, and many Berbers converted to Islam and joined its armies, invading Spain in 711. Resentment at Arab discrimination sparked the Berber Revolt of 740. Independent states followed, including the Rustamids at Tahert, the Midrarids of trading Sijilmasa, and the Idrisids in Morocco from 788.
North Africa.18: The Aghlabid dynasty ruled Ifriqiya (Tunisia) for the Abbasids from 800, rebuilding Kairouan's Great Mosque and conquering Sicily from 827. In Morocco the Idrisids built Fez, where Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in 859. Trans-Saharan caravans carrying gold and salt enriched oasis towns like Sijilmasa.
North Africa.19: The Ismaili Fatimids, backed by Kutama Berbers, overthrew the Aghlabids in 909 and founded a rival caliphate, building a capital at Mahdia. After conquering Egypt in 969 they moved east, leaving the Zirid family to govern Ifriqiya. In the west, Morocco's tribes swung between Fatimid and Umayyad Cordoban influence.
North Africa.20: The Zirids broke with the Fatimids c. 1048, and in revenge Bedouin Banu Hilal tribes migrated west, weakening cities and spreading Arabic. In the western Sahara, Sanhaja Berber reformers founded the Almoravid movement, built Marrakesh c. 1070, and conquered Morocco. They crossed into Spain and defeated Castile at Zallaqa in 1086.
North Africa.21: The Almohads, a reform movement founded by Ibn Tumart among Masmuda Berbers, overthrew the Almoravids, taking Marrakesh in 1147. Under Abd al-Mumin they united the whole Maghreb and al-Andalus, expelling Norman outposts in Tunisia. Their court sponsored philosophers like Averroes and grand mosques like the Koutoubia.
North Africa.22: Defeat by Christian Spain at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 began the Almohad collapse, completed in 1269. Three Berber dynasties divided the Maghreb: the Marinids at Fez, the Zayyanids at Tlemcen, and the Hafsids at Tunis. France's Louis IX died during a crusade against Tunis in 1270.
North Africa.23: Marinid, Zayyanid and Hafsid sultans competed over the Maghreb and its trans-Saharan trade, building elegant madrasas in Fez and Tlemcen. Ibn Battuta of Tangier traveled the known world, and Ibn Khaldun wrote his pioneering history, the Muqaddimah, in 1377. The Black Death struck the region from 1348.
North Africa.24: Portugal captured Ceuta in 1415 and later Tangier, beginning European expansion in Africa. In Morocco the Wattasids replaced the Marinids, while the Hafsids still ruled Tunis. After 1492 Muslims and Jews expelled from Spain settled in Maghrebi cities, bringing skills and resentment, and Spain seized Melilla in 1497.
North Africa.25: Ottoman corsairs led by the Barbarossa brothers took Algiers, then Tripoli in 1551 and Tunis in 1574, making them Ottoman regencies and corsair bases. Morocco stayed independent under the Saadi dynasty, which crushed a Portuguese invasion in 1578. Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur grew rich from sugar and sent an army across the Sahara in 1591.
North Africa.26: The Barbary corsairs of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli raided Mediterranean shipping and coasts, enslaving thousands of Europeans. These regencies became largely self-governing under local deys and beys. Moriscos expelled from Spain in 1609 settled in the region, and in Morocco the Alaouite dynasty took power in 1666, with Moulay Ismail ruling from Meknes.
North Africa.27: Local dynasties consolidated power under loose Ottoman sovereignty: the Husainid beys in Tunis from 1705 and the Karamanli family in Tripoli from 1711, while Algiers was governed by elected deys. Morocco's strong ruler Moulay Ismail died in 1727, plunging the kingdom into decades of succession struggles.
North Africa.28: Sultan Sidi Mohammed ben Abdallah restored order in Morocco, founded the port of Essaouira, and in 1777 became one of the first rulers to recognize the United States. Corsair states collected tribute from European and American shippers for safe passage. Plague hit hard in the 1790s, and Spain gave up Oran in 1792.
North Africa.29: The United States fought the First Barbary War against Tripoli in 1801 to 1805 and the Second Barbary War in 1815 to end tribute payments. A British and Dutch fleet bombarded Algiers in 1816, freeing captives. The age of the Barbary corsairs ended, leaving the regencies weaker and more exposed to European pressure.
North Africa.30: France invaded Algeria in 1830, taking Algiers and launching a brutal conquest. Emir Abd al-Qadir led resistance until 1847, while Morocco's support for him brought defeat at Isly in 1844. The Ottomans reimposed direct rule on Tripoli in 1835, and Tunisia's Ahmad Bey abolished slavery in 1846.
North Africa.31: France conquered Kabylia in 1857 and encouraged European settlers to take Algerian land; the Mokrani revolt of 1871 was crushed. Tunisia adopted the Arab world's first constitution in 1861 but fell into debt to European creditors. Spain defeated Morocco in 1860, and the Sanusi Sufi order spread across Libya's desert.
North Africa.32: France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881, adding to its Algerian colony, where settlers now held the best land and political power. Morocco's Sultan Hassan I worked to modernize and play European powers against each other to stay independent. Libya remained an Ottoman province, with the Sanusi order influential inland.
North Africa.33: Morocco became the focus of European rivalry: Germany's Kaiser visited Tangier in 1905, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 gave France and Spain special roles. French troops occupied Oujda and bombarded Casablanca in 1907. Algeria and Tunisia lived under settler-dominated French rule, while Libya stayed Ottoman.
North Africa.34: Italy seized Libya from the Ottomans in 1911 to 1912, facing fierce Arab and Sanusi resistance. In 1912 France made most of Morocco a protectorate under Resident-General Lyautey, with Spain taking the north. Hundreds of thousands of North Africans served or labored for France in the First World War.
North Africa.35: In Spanish Morocco, Abd el-Krim crushed a Spanish army at Annual in 1921 and founded a Rif Republic until French and Spanish forces defeated him in 1926. Italy waged a brutal reconquest of Libya against Omar Mukhtar's guerrillas. Tunisian nationalists formed the Destour party in 1920.
North Africa.36: Italy hanged Omar Mukhtar in 1931, confined Libyans in camps, and brought in Italian settlers. Bourguiba founded Tunisia's Neo-Destour party in 1934, and Messali Hadj led Algerian nationalism. France lavishly celebrated a century in Algeria in 1930, and in 1936 Franco launched the Spanish Civil War from Spanish Morocco.
North Africa.37: The Second World War brought desert battles to Libya, including the long siege of Tobruk, and Allied landings in Morocco and Algeria in Operation Torch in 1942. Roosevelt and Churchill met at Casablanca in 1943. Nationalist hopes rose, but French forces massacred thousands of Algerians after the Sétif protests of 1945.
North Africa.38: Libya became independent in 1951 as a kingdom under Idris al-Sanusi. Algeria's National Liberation Front began a war against France in 1954 that killed hundreds of thousands. Morocco under Mohammed V and Tunisia under Bourguiba won independence in 1956, while oil was discovered in Libya in 1959.
North Africa.39: Algeria won independence in 1962, and about a million European settlers fled; Ben Bella led until Boumediene's coup in 1965. Hassan II ruled Morocco firmly from 1961, and Algeria and Morocco fought the brief Sand War in 1963. Oil enriched Libya, where Muammar Gaddafi overthrew the monarchy in 1969.
North Africa.40: Gaddafi used oil wealth to fund his 'Green Book' revolution and foreign causes. Algeria nationalized its oil and gas in 1971 under a socialist one-party state. Morocco's 1975 Green March claimed Western Sahara from Spain, starting a long war with the Algerian-backed Polisario Front, while Bourguiba aged in power in Tunisia.
North Africa.41: The United States bombed Libya in 1986, and the Lockerbie bombing of 1988 deepened Gaddafi's isolation. Ben Ali replaced Bourguiba in Tunisia in 1987. Falling oil prices sparked riots in Algeria in 1988, forcing multiparty reforms, and the five Maghreb states formed the Arab Maghreb Union in 1989.
North Africa.42: Algeria's army cancelled 1992 elections that Islamists were winning, triggering a civil war that killed perhaps 150,000 people. Libya endured UN sanctions over Lockerbie. A 1991 ceasefire froze the Western Sahara conflict, and in Morocco Mohammed VI succeeded his father Hassan II in 1999 with promises of reform.
North Africa.43: Algeria's President Bouteflika offered amnesties as the civil war wound down, though al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb kept fighting in the Sahara. Gaddafi gave up weapons programs in 2003 and returned to international favor. Morocco expanded women's rights in 2004, and migration across the Mediterranean to Europe increased.
North Africa.44: A Tunisian street vendor's self-immolation sparked the Arab Spring in 2010, ousting Ben Ali; Tunisia adopted a democratic constitution in 2014. NATO-backed rebels overthrew Gaddafi in 2011, but Libya split into rival governments. Morocco amended its constitution in 2011, and Algeria's Hirak protests ended Bouteflika's rule in 2019.
North Africa.45: Tunisia's President Kais Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and concentrated power, reversing its democratic gains. Libya remained divided between rival eastern and western authorities, and floods in Derna killed thousands in 2023. Morocco normalized ties with Israel in 2020, gained US recognition over Western Sahara, and suffered a deadly earthquake in 2023.

West Africa.0: Hunter-gatherers lived across West Africa's forests and savannas for tens of thousands of years. During the humid 'Green Sahara' period, communities fished and hunted around lakes now gone, and some of the world's earliest pottery was made at Ounjougou in Mali c. 9400 BC. Later, cattle herders spread across the Sahara before it dried.
West Africa.1: As the Sahara turned to desert, herders and their cattle moved south into the Sahel. Farmers of the savanna were domesticating pearl millet, while forest peoples relied on yams and oil palm. The Kintampo culture of Ghana combined farming, herding and stone tools, and stone villages began at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania.
West Africa.2: At Dhar Tichitt, herders and millet farmers built large walled stone villages, an early complex society in the Sahel. African rice was being cultivated along the Niger, and the Kintampo culture flourished in Ghana. Near the Nigeria and Cameroon borderlands, Bantu-speaking peoples began the long expansion that would spread their languages across Africa.
West Africa.3: Bantu-speaking farmers spread farming and, increasingly, iron-working eastward and southward from West-Central Africa over many centuries. In the savanna and forest, village communities grew yams, millet and sorghum. Iron smelting appeared in parts of West Africa by the early first millennium BC, and the Nok culture was developing in central Nigeria.
West Africa.4: The Nok culture of central Nigeria smelted iron and made striking terracotta sculptures of human heads and figures, among the oldest in sub-Saharan Africa. Iron tools helped farmers clear land and grow more food. Across the region, villages of farmers and herders lived under local chiefs and lineage elders rather than large states.
West Africa.5: The Nok culture continued to flourish in central Nigeria, producing terracottas and iron at sites like Taruga. Iron-working spread among neighboring peoples, making hoes and weapons more widely available. To the north, the Garamantes of the Libyan Sahara traded with Sahel peoples, while Sahel villages grew millet and herded livestock.
West Africa.6: Farming and iron-working villages spread through the savanna and forest, and settlements such as Dia on the inland Niger Delta grew. The Nok culture remained a major artistic and technological center in Nigeria. Societies were largely organized around kinship, with craft specialists such as smiths gaining special status.
West Africa.7: Jenne-jeno was founded c. 250 BC on the inland Niger Delta in Mali, growing into one of sub-Saharan Africa's earliest known towns. Its people fished, farmed rice, worked iron and traded along the river, apparently without a single ruler. The Nok culture continued in Nigeria, and iron-using farmers expanded across the region.
West Africa.8: Jenne-jeno and neighboring settlements grew as trading hubs where fishers, farmers and craftspeople exchanged rice, fish, iron and copper. Specialized groups lived in clusters of villages that formed a town without a palace or king. Across the forest and savanna, iron-working farming communities continued to expand.
West Africa.9: Towns along the Niger, including Jenne-jeno, prospered from regional trade in food, iron and salt. The Nok culture was beginning to wane in Nigeria. Contact across the Sahara was limited but real, as Saharan peoples like the Garamantes linked the Sahel to the Roman Mediterranean world.
West Africa.10: Iron-working farming societies now covered much of West Africa, from the Senegal River to the Lake Chad basin. The Nok terracotta tradition faded in this period. Jenne-jeno kept growing, and village communities were organized by kin groups, age sets and ritual leaders rather than kingdoms.
West Africa.11: The camel, introduced to the Sahara from the east, gradually made long desert crossings more practical. Jenne-jeno expanded and traded in copper, salt and stone from distant sources. In Senegambia, people began raising stone circles over burials, and the Soninke peoples of the western Sahel were laying foundations for later states.
West Africa.12: Camel herding spread through the Sahara, and desert Berber groups began to act as middlemen between the Sahel and North Africa. Jenne-jeno became a large town with satellite villages. Among the Soninke, chiefs gained power from controlling trade in gold, salt and slaves, setting the stage for the first great Sahel empire.
West Africa.13: The Ghana Empire, called Wagadu by its Soninke founders, emerged in the region between the Senegal and Niger rivers. Its kings controlled trade routes linking the gold fields to the south with salt from the Sahara. Camel caravans opened regular trans-Saharan trade, linking West Africa to North Africa.
West Africa.14: Ghana grew stronger by taxing gold and salt passing through its territory and by commanding cavalry and iron-armed soldiers. Jenne-jeno flourished as a river trading city, and settlements like Gao developed on the middle Niger. In Senegambia, the building of megalithic stone circles continued.
West Africa.15: Ghana extended its influence over neighboring peoples of the Sahel. Gao on the Niger was growing as a trading center, and farther east, peoples near Lake Chad were forming the communities that would become Kanem. Saharan Berbers such as the Sanhaja controlled desert routes between the Sahel and the north.
West Africa.16: Ghana's kings, ruling from towns in the western Sahel, prospered from gold and salt trade. After the Arab conquest of North Africa, Muslim merchants increasingly organized the trans-Saharan caravans. The Kanem kingdom was taking shape northeast of Lake Chad, and Gao grew as a Niger River market.
West Africa.17: Arab writers first mentioned Ghana in the 700s, calling it a land of gold. Trading towns like Sijilmasa in Morocco, founded in 757, linked caravans to the Sahel. Kanem emerged as a state near Lake Chad, and Gao and Takrur on the Senegal River grew through trans-Saharan trade.
West Africa.18: Ghana dominated the western Sahel's gold trade, and Muslim merchants settled in its towns. In southeastern Nigeria, the Igbo-Ukwu culture produced remarkably intricate bronze castings and imported glass beads, showing complex society and long-distance trade. Kanem expanded near Lake Chad, and Gao rose on the Niger.
West Africa.19: Ghana stood at its height, its king famed in Arabic sources for vast gold and a large army. Its capital, probably Koumbi Saleh, had a royal town and a separate Muslim merchant quarter. Igbo-Ukwu bronze-making flourished in Nigeria, and Kanem and Gao grew as trading kingdoms.
West Africa.20: The geographer al-Bakri described Ghana's wealth and court in 1068. The Almoravid movement from the western Sahara pressured Ghana, which began to weaken. Islam spread among Sahel rulers: Takrur's king converted, Gao's rulers were Muslim, and Kanem's king Hummay embraced Islam c. 1085. In the forest, Ife was rising.
West Africa.21: Ghana declined as trade routes shifted and vassal states broke away, including the Sosso kingdom. In Yoruba country, the city of Ife became a sacred and political center, producing naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads. Hausa city-states such as Kano were forming in northern Nigeria, while Kanem remained powerful.
West Africa.22: Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru and founded the Mali Empire in 1235, controlling the gold trade from the upper Niger. Mali's kings, the mansas, ruled a vast realm of many peoples. Kanem reached its height near Lake Chad, Ife flourished, and the Benin kingdom took shape in the forest.
West Africa.23: Mali was at its peak; Mansa Musa's lavish pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 made its gold famous across the Islamic world and Europe. Timbuktu became a center of trade and Islamic scholarship, with mosques like Djinguereber. Ibn Battuta visited in 1352, Ife and Benin flourished, and Kanem's rulers moved to Bornu.
West Africa.24: Mali weakened as Tuareg took Timbuktu in 1433 and Songhai rose under Sunni Ali from 1464, building a vast empire based at Gao. Portuguese sailors reached the Gold Coast and built Elmina in 1482. Benin expanded under Oba Ewuare, and the Hausa cities and Bornu grew stronger.
West Africa.25: Songhai reached its peak under Askia Muhammad, ruling a vast empire with Timbuktu a renowned center of learning. A Moroccan army with firearms destroyed Songhai at Tondibi in 1591. Bornu prospered under Idris Alooma, Benin traded with the Portuguese, and the Atlantic slave trade grew along the coast.
West Africa.26: With Songhai gone, the Sahel fragmented, and Moroccan-descended rulers held Timbuktu. On the coast the Atlantic slave trade expanded rapidly as Dutch, English and French joined the Portuguese. New kingdoms built on firearms and trade rose, including Asante c. 1670 and Dahomey, while the Oyo Empire expanded with cavalry.
West Africa.27: Asante, unified under Osei Tutu and the sacred Golden Stool, expanded under Opoku Ware. Dahomey conquered the slaving port of Ouidah in 1727 but paid tribute to Oyo. The Bambara kingdom of Segou rose on the Niger, and the Atlantic slave trade neared its peak, carrying tens of thousands of captives a year.
West Africa.28: The Atlantic slave trade reached its height, deeply shaping coastal kingdoms such as Asante, Dahomey and Oyo. Islamic reform movements created new states in Futa Jallon and Futa Toro. Britain founded Freetown in Sierra Leone for freed slaves in 1787 to 1792, and the explorer Mungo Park traveled the Niger in 1795.
West Africa.29: Usman dan Fodio's Fulani jihad from 1804 overthrew Hausa kings and created the Sokoto Caliphate, one of Africa's largest states. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and patrolled the coast against slavers. Freetown became a British colony, and freed African Americans began settling Liberia in 1822.
West Africa.30: The Oyo Empire collapsed c. 1835, unleashing Yoruba wars and the rise of new cities such as Ibadan and Abeokuta. Seku Amadu's Masina Caliphate ruled the inland Niger Delta. Trade shifted toward palm oil for Europe's factories, and Liberia declared independence in 1847, becoming Africa's first modern republic.
West Africa.31: Al-Hajj Umar Tall's jihad built the Tukulor Empire across the western Sudan in the 1850s and 1860s. France expanded from Senegal under Governor Faidherbe, founding Dakar in 1857, while Britain annexed Lagos in 1861. British troops burned the Asante capital Kumasi in 1874 during the Anglo-Asante War.
West Africa.32: Britain made the Gold Coast a colony in 1874, and after the Berlin Conference European powers raced to conquer the interior. Samori Touré resisted the French until his capture in 1898, Dahomey fell in 1894, and the British sacked Benin City in 1897, looting its bronzes. Only Liberia stayed independent.
West Africa.33: Britain conquered the Sokoto Caliphate in 1903 and crushed Asante's last revolt, led by Yaa Asantewaa, in 1900. France ruled French West Africa as a federation from Dakar. Colonial rule brought forced labor, taxes and railways, and farmers turned to cash crops such as cocoa, making the Gold Coast a leading producer.
West Africa.34: Britain merged its territories into Nigeria in 1914 under Lugard's indirect rule through local chiefs. During the First World War, Allied troops took German Togoland and Kamerun, and France recruited many tirailleurs sénégalais. Blaise Diagne became the first black African deputy in the French parliament in 1914.
West Africa.35: Colonial governments ruled through chiefs while expanding cash crops like cocoa, peanuts and palm oil. Western-educated Africans formed the National Congress of British West Africa in 1920 to demand a voice, and Herbert Macaulay led early Nigerian politics. Liberia leased vast land to the Firestone rubber company in 1926.
West Africa.36: The Great Depression slashed crop prices, and Gold Coast farmers staged cocoa hold-ups in 1937 to 1938. Nnamdi Azikiwe's newspapers spread nationalist ideas in Nigeria, while in Paris Léopold Senghor and others launched the Négritude movement celebrating African culture. Colonial rule still seemed firmly entrenched.
West Africa.37: The Second World War drew West African soldiers to fight in Burma and Europe. After the war, the French granted limited political rights, and the RDA party formed in 1946; French troops killed returning soldiers at Thiaroye in 1944. Riots in Accra in 1948 led to Kwame Nkrumah's mass nationalist party in 1949.
West Africa.38: Nationalist parties won elections under new constitutions as colonial rule loosened. Nkrumah led Ghana, formerly the Gold Coast, to independence in 1957, the first sub-Saharan colony to break free. Guinea, under Sékou Touré, voted to leave the French community in 1958 and became independent immediately.
West Africa.39: Nigeria and most of French West Africa became independent in 1960, led by figures such as Senghor in Senegal. Military coups soon followed, including Nkrumah's overthrow in 1966. Nigeria's Civil War over Biafra's secession in 1967 to 1970 killed perhaps a million people, many from famine.
West Africa.40: Oil wealth transformed Nigeria while its military governments ruled. West African states formed ECOWAS in 1975 to promote trade and cooperation. A severe Sahel drought in the early 1970s caused famine. Guinea-Bissau won independence from Portugal in 1974, and Jerry Rawlings first seized power in Ghana in 1979.
West Africa.41: Falling commodity prices and debt forced many states into harsh structural adjustment programs. Samuel Doe seized power in Liberia in 1980, and Thomas Sankara led a revolutionary government in Burkina Faso until his murder in 1987. Military rule persisted in Nigeria, and Liberia's civil war began in 1989.
West Africa.42: Brutal civil wars engulfed Liberia and Sierra Leone, fueled by diamonds and child soldiers, as a Nigerian-led ECOWAS force intervened. Nigeria's dictator Sani Abacha executed activist Ken Saro-Wiwa in 1995, then civilian rule returned in 1999. Elsewhere, countries like Benin and Mali held multiparty elections.
West Africa.43: The wars in Sierra Leone and Liberia ended in 2002 and 2003, and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected female head of state in 2006. Côte d'Ivoire was split by civil war. Nigeria and Ghana held regular elections, while the Boko Haram insurgency erupted in northeastern Nigeria in 2009.
West Africa.44: Islamist rebels seized northern Mali in 2012, prompting French intervention, and Boko Haram kidnapped the Chibok schoolgirls in 2014. The Ebola epidemic of 2014 to 2016 killed over 11,000 people in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Nigeria saw its first peaceful transfer to an opposition president in 2015.
West Africa.45: Military juntas seized power in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger from 2020 to 2023, expelled French troops, and turned to Russia, forming an Alliance of Sahel States outside ECOWAS. Jihadist violence spread across the Sahel. Coastal states such as Senegal and Ghana held competitive elections, while Nigeria faced inflation and insecurity.

East Africa.0: East Africa is the cradle of humankind: the hominin 'Lucy' lived in Ethiopia 3.2 million years ago, and some of the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils come from Omo, Ethiopia. Later hunter-gatherers fished the then-larger lakes of the Rift Valley and Nile, and cattle herding spread into Sudan before 5000 BC.
East Africa.1: In Nubia, along the Nile south of Egypt, the A-Group culture traded with early Egypt, and the Kerma culture arose c. 2500 BC, becoming the first kingdom of Kush. Herders brought cattle, sheep and goats into the Kenyan Rift Valley, while Ethiopian highlanders began cultivating local crops such as teff and ensete.
East Africa.2: The kingdom of Kush, centered at Kerma, became a wealthy rival to Egypt before New Kingdom pharaohs conquered Nubia c. 1500 BC and ruled it for centuries. Egypt traded for incense, ebony and exotic animals with the Land of Punt, probably on the southern Red Sea coast. Pastoralists spread through the highlands of Kenya and Tanzania.
East Africa.3: After Egypt withdrew, a new kingdom of Kush arose at Napata, and its king Piye conquered Egypt c. 744 BC, ruling as pharaohs until expelled by Assyria. In northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, the kingdom of D'mt built temples at Yeha with South Arabian links. Iron-working farmers appeared around the Great Lakes.
East Africa.4: Driven from Egypt, the Kushite kings ruled from Napata and increasingly from Meroë farther south, especially after an Egyptian raid on Napata in 593 BC. The D'mt kingdom continued in the Ethiopian highlands. Around Lake Victoria, Bantu-speaking farmers of the Urewe tradition were smelting iron and growing crops.
East Africa.5: The Kushite kingdom flourished on the Nile, its royal tombs topped by steep pyramids. Herodotus wrote of these 'long-lived Ethiopians', and a Persian army had failed to conquer them. D'mt faded in the Ethiopian highlands, while iron-using Bantu-speaking communities expanded around the Great Lakes.
East Africa.6: Meroë grew into Kush's capital and a major center of iron-working, surrounded by slag heaps and fields of sorghum. Its rulers traded ivory, gold and ebony with Ptolemaic Egypt. In the Great Lakes region, Bantu-speaking farmers continued spreading iron tools, cattle and crops among existing hunting and herding peoples.
East Africa.7: Under rulers like Arkamani, Meroë developed its own culture, including the Meroitic script and temples to the lion god Apedemak at Musawwarat es-Sufra. Ptolemaic Egypt sent ships to the Red Sea coast to hunt war elephants. Bantu-speaking farmers moved toward the East African coast.
East Africa.8: The Meroitic kingdom prospered, ruled at times by powerful queens called Kandakes, such as Shanakdakhete. Its pyramids and temples blended Egyptian and local traditions. Along the coast and in the interior, iron-working farming villages multiplied, and Red Sea trade linked the region to the Mediterranean and Arabia.
East Africa.9: The Kushite queen Amanirenas fought Rome after it annexed Egypt, and a 21 BC treaty ended the war on favorable terms for Meroë. Communities in the Ethiopian highlands were forming the polity that would become Aksum. Iron-working Bantu-speaking farmers were spreading along the East African coast.
East Africa.10: A Greek merchant's guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, described the Red Sea port of Adulis and the trading town of Rhapta on the Swahili coast. Aksum was growing in the Ethiopian highlands, and Meroë remained powerful on the Nile. Nero sent explorers up the Nile to investigate Kush.
East Africa.11: The Kingdom of Aksum rose in northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, growing rich on Red Sea trade in ivory and gold. Its rulers erected tall carved stone stelae. Meroë continued on the Nile, while coastal towns like Rhapta traded with Roman and Arabian merchants, and Bantu-speaking farmers settled ever more widely.
East Africa.12: Aksum minted its own coins and was counted by the Persian prophet Mani among the four great kingdoms of the world. It controlled trade between the Roman world, Arabia and India. Meroë was declining as trade shifted to the Red Sea, and farming communities spread through the interior.
East Africa.13: King Ezana of Aksum adopted Christianity c. 330, making it one of the first Christian states. Aksum campaigned against the declining Meroë c. 350, and the Kushite kingdom collapsed. In Nubia new states emerged: Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia. On the coast and around the Great Lakes, Bantu farming communities expanded.
East Africa.14: Christianity deepened in Aksum as the Nine Saints, monks from the Roman world, founded monasteries, and the Bible was translated into Ge'ez. Aksum's stelae and palaces showed its wealth. In Nubia, successor kingdoms buried rulers in rich mound tombs, while farming villages grew along the East African coast.
East Africa.15: Aksum's King Kaleb invaded Himyar in Yemen c. 525, briefly extending power across the Red Sea. Missionaries from Byzantium converted the Nubian kingdoms to Christianity from c. 543. On the coast, early farming and fishing villages with distinctive pottery were the ancestors of later Swahili towns.
East Africa.16: Aksum's king sheltered early Muslim refugees from Mecca in 615, but Aksum declined as Arab expansion shifted Red Sea trade. In Nubia, Makuria defeated Arab invaders and in 652 signed the Baqt treaty with Muslim Egypt, a trade pact that lasted centuries. Makuria absorbed neighboring Nobadia.
East Africa.17: Aksum faded and Ethiopian Christian power moved south into the highlands. Christian Makuria flourished, decorating churches like the cathedral at Faras with vivid paintings. On the coast, Swahili towns such as Shanga built early mosques as Islam arrived with Indian Ocean traders seeking ivory and other goods.
East Africa.18: Swahili towns grew along the coast, trading ivory, gold and enslaved people across the Indian Ocean. Enslaved East Africans, called Zanj, rose in a massive revolt in Iraq from 869 to 883. Makuria and Alodia were thriving Christian Nubian kingdoms, while Ethiopia's history in this era is poorly recorded.
East Africa.19: Arab traveler al-Masudi described the Swahili coast and its gold trade c. 916, and according to tradition Kilwa was founded around this time. Ethiopian tradition tells of a queen, Gudit, who sacked Aksum c. 960. Makuria was at its height in Nubia, and pastoral and farming peoples spread inland.
East Africa.20: Swahili towns from Mogadishu to Kilwa adopted Islam and traded ivory, gold and timber with Arabia, Persia and India. Gold from Zimbabwe passed through Sofala to Kilwa. Christian Nubian kingdoms remained strong, and in the Ethiopian highlands, Christian rulers reorganized after Aksum's fall.
East Africa.21: Swahili city-states such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Zanzibar thrived on Indian Ocean trade, building coral stone mosques and houses. The Zagwe dynasty took power in Ethiopia c. 1137. Mogadishu was a major port, and in the Great Lakes region, earthwork sites like Ntusi show growing cattle-based states.
East Africa.22: King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty built churches carved from solid rock. In 1270 Yekuno Amlak founded the Solomonic dynasty, claiming descent from Solomon and Sheba. Kilwa grew rich controlling the gold trade from Sofala, while Mamluk Egypt weakened Christian Makuria and Muslim sultanates rose in Ethiopia's east.
East Africa.23: Emperor Amda Seyon expanded Ethiopia against the Muslim sultanate of Ifat, and the Kebra Nagast legend glorified the dynasty. Ibn Battuta admired Kilwa and Mogadishu in 1331, where Kilwa built the palace of Husuni Kubwa. Makuria collapsed as Arab nomads moved into Sudan, and kingdoms formed in the Great Lakes.
East Africa.24: Ethiopia's Emperor Zara Yaqob strengthened the church and the crown. Swahili towns traded with Asia, and Chinese admiral Zheng He's fleet visited in 1418 to 1419. Vasco da Gama reached Mombasa and Malindi in 1498. Inland, the kingdoms of Bunyoro and Buganda were taking shape.
East Africa.25: The Portuguese sacked Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505 and built Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593 to control the coast. In Ethiopia, Ahmad Gragn of Adal invaded from 1529 until Ethiopians with Portuguese help defeated him in 1543. Oromo peoples migrated north, and the Funj Sultanate ruled Sudan from Sennar.
East Africa.26: Emperor Fasilides founded Gondar as Ethiopia's capital in 1636 and expelled the Jesuits after a disastrous attempt to convert the country to Catholicism. Omani Arabs captured Fort Jesus in 1698, ending Portuguese power north of Mozambique. Buganda and Bunyoro competed in the Great Lakes, and the Funj ruled Sudan.
East Africa.27: Omani Arabs dominated the Swahili coast, though local families like the Mazrui of Mombasa acted largely independently. Ethiopian emperors at Gondar built castles and churches but struggled with regional nobles. The Funj Sultanate ruled Sudan, and Buganda expanded its power around Lake Victoria.
East Africa.28: Ethiopia entered the Zemene Mesafint, the Era of the Princes, from 1769, as regional warlords overshadowed powerless emperors. The Funj Sultanate weakened in Sudan. Buganda and Rwanda grew stronger, centralizing under powerful kings, while ivory and slave trades linked the interior to the coast.
East Africa.29: Muhammad Ali's Egypt conquered Sudan from 1820, founding Khartoum as its capital and raiding for slaves and gold. Ethiopia remained divided among rival princes. On the coast, Sayyid Said of Oman strengthened his hold on the Swahili towns, while Buganda's kings expanded their power.
East Africa.30: Sultan Said of Oman moved his capital to Zanzibar in 1840, building a commercial empire on clove plantations worked by enslaved people. Arab and Swahili caravans pushed deep inland for ivory and captives. European missionaries arrived, and Egyptian rule extended through Sudan, while Ethiopia stayed fragmented.
East Africa.31: Tewodros II reunited Ethiopia from 1855 but died at Magdala during a British expedition in 1868. European explorers like Speke and Burton sought the Nile's source. Under British pressure, Zanzibar closed its slave market in 1873, while Buganda's Kabaka Mutesa I welcomed foreign traders and missionaries.
East Africa.32: Britain, Germany and Italy partitioned the region, but Menelik II's Ethiopia crushed Italy at Adwa in 1896 and stayed independent. In Sudan, the Mahdist uprising took Khartoum in 1885 until Anglo-Egyptian forces won at Omdurman in 1898. A rinderpest epidemic devastated cattle-herding peoples.
East Africa.33: Britain's Uganda Railway reached Lake Victoria in 1901, bringing white settlers to Kenya's highlands. In German East Africa, the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 to 1907 was crushed, causing famine and many deaths. Menelik II modernized Ethiopia from Addis Ababa, and Sudan was ruled by an Anglo-Egyptian condominium.
East Africa.34: The First World War brought a long campaign in East Africa as Germany's Lettow-Vorbeck evaded British forces, while many African porters died of disease and hunger. In Ethiopia, Lij Iyasu was deposed in 1916, and Ras Tafari became regent. British forces defeated the Somali Dervish leader Sayyid Muhammad in 1920.
East Africa.35: Britain took over Tanganyika and Belgium Rwanda-Burundi as League of Nations mandates. Ethiopia joined the League in 1923 under regent Ras Tafari. In Kenya, early African protest leaders such as Harry Thuku challenged settler privileges, and Sudan's huge Gezira cotton scheme opened in 1925.
East Africa.36: Ras Tafari was crowned Emperor Haile Selassie in 1930 and pursued modernization. Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 to 1936, using poison gas, and joined it with Eritrea and Somalia as Italian East Africa. Haile Selassie's appeal to the League of Nations went unanswered, while Jomo Kenyatta campaigned in Britain.
East Africa.37: British and Commonwealth forces drove Italy out of Ethiopia in 1941, and Haile Selassie returned to his throne. Eritrea and Italian Somaliland came under British administration. In Kenya, land pressure and settler dominance fueled African political organization, while colonial development schemes expanded.
East Africa.38: Kenya's Mau Mau uprising of 1952 to 1960 was brutally suppressed, with mass detentions. Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia in 1952. Sudan won independence in 1956, but civil war had begun in the south in 1955. In Rwanda, the Hutu revolution of 1959 overthrew the Tutsi monarchy.
East Africa.39: Somalia, Tanganyika, Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda and Burundi won independence between 1960 and 1963. Tanganyika merged with Zanzibar as Tanzania in 1964, and Julius Nyerere pursued African socialism. Eritrean rebels began a war against Ethiopian rule in 1961, while Kenyatta led Kenya.
East Africa.40: Idi Amin seized Uganda in 1971, expelled its Asian community, and killed many thousands before Tanzania ousted him in 1979. Ethiopia's monarchy was overthrown in 1974 by the Marxist Derg, which waged the Red Terror and fought Somalia over the Ogaden. Sudan's first civil war ended in 1972.
East Africa.41: A catastrophic famine struck Ethiopia in 1983 to 1985, worsened by war and policy, prompting the Live Aid concerts. Sudan's second civil war began in 1983. Yoweri Museveni took power in Uganda in 1986, Kenya became a one-party state, and HIV/AIDS spread widely in the region.
East Africa.42: Ethiopia's Derg fell in 1991, and Eritrea gained independence in 1993. Somalia's government collapsed in 1991, leading to famine and a failed UN mission. In Rwanda, extremists killed about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in 1994. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a bloody border war from 1998.
East Africa.43: Sudan's Darfur conflict from 2003 killed hundreds of thousands, while a 2005 peace deal ended the north-south civil war. Kenya's disputed 2007 election sparked deadly violence. Ethiopian troops intervened in Somalia in 2006, fueling the al-Shabaab insurgency, and Rwanda rebuilt rapidly under Paul Kagame.
East Africa.44: South Sudan won independence in 2011 but fell into civil war in 2013. Ethiopia's economy boomed as it built the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, and Abiy Ahmed made peace with Eritrea in 2018, winning a Nobel Prize. Protests toppled Sudan's Omar al-Bashir in 2019, and al-Shabaab attacked Kenya.
East Africa.45: Ethiopia's Tigray War from 2020 to 2022 killed hundreds of thousands. Sudan descended into civil war between its army and the RSF militia in 2023, creating one of the world's largest displacement and hunger crises. Kenya saw youth-led protests in 2024, and Ethiopia completed its great Nile dam.

South Africa.0: Southern Africa holds deep human history: early hominins left fossils at Sterkfontein and Taung, and c. 75,000 years ago people at Blombos Cave engraved ochre and made shell beads, some of the earliest symbolic art. In later millennia, ancestors of the San lived as hunter-gatherers across the region.
South Africa.1: Southern Africa was home to hunter-gatherers, ancestors of today's San, who lived in small mobile bands. They hunted antelope with bows and poisoned arrows, gathered plants, and harvested shellfish on the coasts. Their rich rock paintings and engravings in places like the Drakensberg and Matobo Hills depict animals and spiritual rituals.
South Africa.2: San hunter-gatherers continued to live across southern Africa, using small, finely made stone tools and ostrich-eggshell beads, which they also traded. Families moved seasonally across deserts, grasslands and coasts. No farming or herding had yet arrived, and there were no states, only bands bound by kinship and sharing.
South Africa.3: Hunter-gatherer bands, ancestors of the San, occupied the region, from the Kalahari to the Cape. Far to the north, Bantu-speaking farmers were beginning to spread iron-working and agriculture through central Africa, but they had not yet reached the south. Rock art remained central to San religious life.
South Africa.4: San hunter-gatherers continued their long-established way of life, painting eland and trance dances on rock shelters. Coastal groups fished and gathered shellfish, leaving large shell middens. Meanwhile, iron-working Bantu-speaking farmers were establishing themselves around the Great Lakes, far to the north.
South Africa.5: Southern Africa remained the land of hunter-gatherers, whose deep knowledge of plants, water sources and animal behavior allowed them to thrive in harsh environments such as the Kalahari. Their societies were egalitarian, and sharing food and gifts bound bands together across wide territories.
South Africa.6: Hunter-gatherer communities, ancestors of the San, occupied mountains, plains and shores across the region. Coastal peoples used stone fish traps and gathered abundant shellfish. Farming and herding peoples were still far to the north, and southern Africa's population remained small and widely scattered.
South Africa.7: Domesticated sheep began reaching the far north of the region, appearing in Namibia c. 200 BC, probably through contact with herders farther north. Most people were still San hunter-gatherers. The arrival of livestock started changing how some groups lived, introducing ideas of property and wealth in animals.
South Africa.8: Sheep herding and pottery spread south among some hunter-gatherer groups, giving rise to pastoralist ways of life. These herders were ancestors of the Khoekhoe. San bands continued hunting and gathering, while to the north, Bantu-speaking farmers advanced through the Zambezi region.
South Africa.9: By about 2,000 years ago, sheep had reached the Cape, kept by pastoralists ancestral to the Khoekhoe, who moved with their flocks between seasonal pastures. San hunter-gatherers lived alongside them. North of the Limpopo, iron-using Bantu-speaking farmers were approaching the region.
South Africa.10: Khoekhoe herders grazed sheep and soon cattle across western and southern parts of the region, while San bands hunted and gathered. Iron-working Bantu-speaking farmers spread through Zambia and Malawi, bringing crops like sorghum and millet. Contact between herders, hunters and farmers grew.
South Africa.11: Bantu-speaking farmers began crossing the Zambezi into Zimbabwe and Mozambique, bringing iron tools, pottery, cattle and grain crops. Early farming villages appeared near the Mozambique coast. Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers still occupied most of the south and west.
South Africa.12: Iron-using farmers reached the Limpopo valley and the coast of today's KwaZulu-Natal, building villages of round houses near fertile land. They grew sorghum and millet and herded cattle. These newcomers interacted, traded and sometimes intermarried with San and Khoekhoe peoples.
South Africa.13: Bantu-speaking farmers settled widely across the eastern half of the region, from Zimbabwe to the Eastern Cape, establishing Early Iron Age villages. Cattle were becoming central to wealth and marriage. The drier west remained the domain of Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers.
South Africa.14: Early Iron Age farming communities grew across the eastern grasslands and river valleys, smelting iron and making distinctive pottery. Villages were organized around cattle enclosures. San hunter-gatherers continued living in the mountains and drier lands, sometimes trading game and skins with farmers.
South Africa.15: Farming villages flourished across the east; the Lydenburg Heads, terracotta sculptures from c. 500, show their rich ritual life. Sites like Ndondondwane in KwaZulu-Natal reveal cattle, iron-working and ivory craft. Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers held the Cape and Kalahari.
South Africa.16: Iron Age farming communities continued to grow in what are now Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique and South Africa. Trade on the Mozambique coast, at sites like Chibuene, began linking the interior to Indian Ocean merchants, who offered glass beads and cloth for ivory and other goods.
South Africa.17: Farmers of the Zhizo culture in the Shashe-Limpopo region began trading ivory to the coast for glass beads, linking them to the Indian Ocean economy. Cattle herding and grain farming supported growing villages. Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers lived in the west and south.
South Africa.18: Zhizo farming communities thrived in the Limpopo basin, and the trading town of Schroda grew as an ivory-trading center. In Botswana, the Toutswe culture built hilltop settlements with huge cattle herds. Long-distance trade began to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of chiefs.
South Africa.19: Trade in ivory and other goods with the Swahili coast grew, and Leopard's Kopje farmers took over the Shashe-Limpopo region, founding K2. Cattle and trade wealth increased social inequality. Toutswe chiefdoms prospered in eastern Botswana, while Khoekhoe and San lived across the west.
South Africa.20: K2 grew into a sizable town in the Limpopo valley, its rulers controlling trade in ivory and, increasingly, gold from Zimbabwe's goldfields. Society became more divided between elites and commoners. Elsewhere, farming communities spread south through the grasslands of today's South Africa.
South Africa.21: The capital moved from K2 to Mapungubwe hill, where rulers lived above commoners in a new class-based society, the first state in southern Africa. Gold and ivory went to Kilwa via the coast. On the Zimbabwe plateau, the settlement at Great Zimbabwe was beginning to grow.
South Africa.22: Mapungubwe reached its height, its elite buried with gold objects such as the famous golden rhinoceros, before it was abandoned c. 1290, possibly due to climate change. Power shifted north to Great Zimbabwe, whose rulers took control of the gold trade.
South Africa.23: Great Zimbabwe reached its peak, a stone city of perhaps 10,000 or more people built with mortarless granite walls, including the Great Enclosure. Its Shona-speaking rulers grew rich from cattle and gold exported through Sofala to Kilwa. Chinese porcelain and Persian pottery found there show its global connections.
South Africa.24: Great Zimbabwe declined after c. 1450, as its successor states rose: the Mutapa kingdom in the north and the Torwa state at Khami in the southwest. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and Vasco da Gama sailed past in 1497. Khoekhoe herders held the Cape.
South Africa.25: The Portuguese built forts at Sofala and Mozambique Island and traded with the Mutapa kingdom for gold, sometimes interfering in its politics. A Portuguese conquest attempt in 1569 to 1572 failed. Sotho-Tswana and Nguni-speaking communities expanded on the highveld and in the east.
South Africa.26: The Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station, soon granting land to settlers and importing enslaved people from Asia and Africa. Khoekhoe herders lost land and cattle in wars. On the plateau, the Rozvi under Changamire drove out the Portuguese in the 1690s.
South Africa.27: Dutch settlers, called trekboers, pushed inland from the Cape with their herds, displacing Khoekhoe and San. A smallpox epidemic in 1713 devastated Khoekhoe communities. The Rozvi state ruled the Zimbabwe plateau, while Sotho-Tswana towns and Nguni chiefdoms grew in the interior.
South Africa.28: Trekboer expansion reached the Fish River, leading to the first of many frontier wars with the Xhosa in 1779. Britain seized the Cape from the Dutch in 1795. In the east, Nguni chiefdoms such as the Mthethwa and Ndwandwe grew more powerful as competition for land intensified.
South Africa.29: Britain took permanent control of the Cape in 1806 and brought British settlers in 1820. Shaka built the Zulu Kingdom from 1816, and wars and migrations known as the Mfecane spread across the region. Mzilikazi's Ndebele moved north, and Moshoeshoe founded the Basotho nation at Thaba Bosiu.
South Africa.30: Britain abolished slavery in the Cape in 1834, and many Boers, resenting British rule, set off on the Great Trek into the interior from 1835. They defeated the Zulu at Blood River in 1838. Britain annexed Natal in 1843, and Mzilikazi's Ndebele settled in western Zimbabwe.
South Africa.31: Britain recognized the Boer republics of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State in 1852 and 1854. The Xhosa cattle-killing of 1856 to 1857 brought famine. Basutoland became a British protectorate in 1868, and the discovery of diamonds near Kimberley in 1867 began an industrial revolution.
South Africa.32: The Zulu defeated the British at Isandlwana in 1879 but lost the Anglo-Zulu War. Gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, creating Johannesburg. Cecil Rhodes' company colonized Rhodesia, crushing Ndebele and Shona risings in 1896 to 1897, and the Boer War began in 1899.
South Africa.33: Britain won the Boer War in 1902 after burning farms and confining Boer and African civilians in deadly camps. In German South West Africa, Germany committed genocide against the Herero and Nama from 1904 to 1908. Gandhi led Indian resistance in South Africa, and the Bambatha rebellion was crushed in 1906.
South Africa.34: The Union of South Africa was formed in 1910 under white minority rule, and the African National Congress was founded in 1912 to resist. The 1913 Natives Land Act limited African land ownership to small reserves. During the First World War, South African forces seized German South West Africa.
South Africa.35: White miners' Rand Revolt of 1922 was crushed by force. South Africa ruled South West Africa as a League mandate, and Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing settler colony in 1923. Hertzog's government favored white workers, while the ICU union drew mass support from African workers.
South Africa.36: The Great Depression hit hard, and Hertzog and Smuts merged their parties in 1934. In 1936 laws removed African voters from the Cape rolls and fixed African reserves at a fraction of the land. In Northern Rhodesia, the Copperbelt mining boom drew African workers, who struck in 1935.
South Africa.37: South Africa fought with the Allies in the Second World War, and its industry boomed. Young activists including Mandela formed the ANC Youth League in 1944, and African mineworkers struck in 1946. In 1948 the National Party won power and began making apartheid the law.
South Africa.38: Apartheid laws classified everyone by race, segregated cities and created separate ethnic 'homelands'. The ANC's Defiance Campaign of 1952 and the 1955 Freedom Charter mobilized resistance, met by the Treason Trial. Britain created the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953.
South Africa.39: Police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, and the ANC turned to armed struggle; Mandela was sentenced to life in 1964. South Africa became a republic in 1961. Zambia, Malawi, Botswana and Lesotho gained independence, while Rhodesia's white government declared independence in 1965.
South Africa.40: Student protests in Soweto in 1976 were met with deadly force, and Black Consciousness leader Steve Biko died in police custody in 1977. Mozambique and Angola won independence in 1975, and guerrilla war intensified in Rhodesia, while South Africa declared some homelands 'independent'.
South Africa.41: Zimbabwe became independent in 1980 under Robert Mugabe, whose forces later massacred thousands in Matabeleland. In South Africa, township uprisings and states of emergency met growing international sanctions. South Africa backed wars in Mozambique and Angola, and F. W. de Klerk became president in 1989.
South Africa.42: De Klerk freed Mandela in 1990 and unbanned the ANC, and Namibia gained independence that year. After tense negotiations, South Africa's first multiracial elections in 1994 made Mandela president. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission examined apartheid's crimes, and Mozambique's civil war ended in 1992.
South Africa.43: Thabo Mbeki led South Africa, but his denial of AIDS science worsened a devastating epidemic. In Zimbabwe, land seizures from 2000 and political repression led to economic collapse and hyperinflation by 2008. South Africa's economy grew, and Jacob Zuma became president in 2009.
South Africa.44: South Africa hosted the 2010 World Cup, but police killed 34 striking miners at Marikana in 2012. Mandela died in 2013. Corruption scandals forced Zuma to resign in 2018, and power shortages hit the economy. In Zimbabwe, the army forced Mugabe out in 2017.
South Africa.45: Southern Africa was hit by COVID-19 and deadly unrest in South Africa in 2021. In 2024 the ANC lost its majority for the first time and formed a coalition government, and Botswana's long-ruling party was voted out. An Islamist insurgency troubled northern Mozambique.
